title: Same Fence, Different Garden
premise: Two gardeners each receive twelve fence segments and want the largest rectangular planting area. Their first rectangles enclose different tile counts; rearranging the same segments reveals why equal perimeters need not give equal areas.
hook: They have the same fence. Do they get the same garden?
visible_action: Twelve boundary sticks hinge into one-by-five and three-by-three rectangles as unit squares fill the interiors.
intended_takeaway_or_theme: Perimeter measures a boundary; area measures the enclosed surface.
gate: Use unit-width fences with explicitly labeled idealized dimensions.

style_application.geometry: Exact vector plan and matching 3D blocks
style_application.why: The plan supports counting while the spatial view supports intuition.
style_application.check: Verify identical perimeters, areas, units and source geometry.

editorial_pick.original_reason: Equal fence length and different garden area create an inspectable geometric contrast.
editorial_pick.proposed_first_version: Rearrange the same boundary pieces into two original plots, then tile their interiors using a shared unit.
editorial_pick.gate: Verify perimeter and area independently. Keep units and any grid scale explicit.
